young.html: What would make you happy forever? A pile of money? Being famous? Being the strongest kid in the world? Thomas Aquinas asked this question about 750 years ago, and he tested the answers one by one, like a detective crossing suspects off a list.

young.name: gb-happy-goods
young.cap: Tap each card to see why Aquinas crossed it off. Then press "Aquinas's answer."

young.html: His test was simple: if you want something only to get something else, it cannot be the last thing you want. Money is for buying things. Fame is what other people think, and they can change their minds. Even good feelings come and go. Aquinas decided that only God could fill the human heart completely.

He also wrote about habits. If you practice the piano every day, playing gets easier, until one day it feels natural. Aquinas said being good works the same way. Telling the truth, sharing and being brave become easier each time, until they are part of you. A good habit like that is called a virtue.

The "what for?" game. Write down five things you want. For each one, ask "What do I want it for?" and write the answer. Then ask again about that answer. (Shoes: to play soccer. Soccer: because it's fun with friends. Friends: ...) Where does each chain stop? Do any stop in the same place?

Aquinas wrote about rules and laws too. A good law, he said, has to make sense, has to help everyone and not just the person who made it, and has to be told to people so they know it. Can you think of a family rule that passes all three tests?

full.text: The Second Part: how to live

full.html: The First Part of the Summa was about God and creation. The Second Part, the largest, is about human beings as free agents: what we aim at, how we act, and what helps or harms us on the way. Aquinas divides it in two. The First Part of the Second Part (in Latin, Prima Secundae) gives the general principles: happiness, human acts, feelings, habits, virtues, sin, law and grace. This rung covers it. The next rung turns to particular virtues.

Aquinas begins where Aristotle's Ethics begins. Everything we do, we do for some end, and the ends form chains: I study to pass, pass to graduate, graduate to work. The chain cannot go on forever, so there is a last end, wanted for itself. Everyone agrees, he says, that this last end is happiness. The hard part is saying what happiness is.

full.name: gb-happy-goods
full.cap: The eight candidates of Question 2, with Aquinas's reason for rejecting each (in our own words).

full.text: It is impossible for man's happiness to consist in wealth.
full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part of the Second Part, Question 2, Article 1
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.html: One by one he rules out wealth, honor, fame, power, health and beauty, pleasure, and even the goods of the soul such as knowledge. His reason in the last article is the deepest: the human will reaches for goodness without limit, so no limited good can bring it to rest.

full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part of the Second Part, Question 2, Article 8
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province

full.html: Perfect happiness, he concludes (Question 3), is seeing God as he is, which he believes belongs to the life to come. But he does not dismiss this life. There is a real, imperfect happiness here, found above all in knowing the truth and in living virtuously, helped by friends and by enough of the goods of the body.

items: Human acts (Questions 6 to 21): an act is fully human when it comes from reason and will. Whether it is good depends on what is done, why, and in what circumstances.

Passions, or feelings (Questions 22 to 48): Aquinas lists eleven. Six concern good and evil simply: love and hatred, desire and aversion, joy and sorrow. Five concern good or evil that is hard to reach or avoid: hope and despair, fear and daring, and anger. Feelings are not bad in themselves; they become good or bad by how reason guides them.
Habits (Questions 49 to 54): a habit is a settled way of being, built up by repeated acts, that makes action easy and sure.

full.html: A virtue is a good habit (Question 55). Aquinas sorts them: intellectual virtues perfect the mind (wisdom, understanding, knowledge, art, and prudence); moral virtues perfect our choices and feelings; and the theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, direct us to God and are, he holds, given by God. Four moral virtues are "cardinal," or hinge, virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude (courage) and temperance.
Following Aristotle, he says a moral virtue lies in a mean between two extremes, set by reason (Question 64). Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness.

full.title: Finding the mean
full.q: Aquinas, like Aristotle, puts each moral virtue between a "too little" and a "too much." Name the extremes around generosity with money.
steps: Ask what the virtue is about: giving and spending money.
Too little giving: stinginess. Too much: wastefulness.
The mean is not a fixed amount; it is what reason judges right for this person, here and now.
full.a: Stinginess and wastefulness; generosity is the mean between them.

full.html: Near the end of the First Part of the Second Part come the questions on law (Questions 90 to 108), still among the most read pages of the Summa. Aquinas first asks what a law is. Four articles give four parts of an answer.

full.text: ... it is nothing else than an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated.
full.work: Summa Theologica, First Part of the Second Part, Question 90, Article 4
full.author: Thomas Aquinas
full.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
full.note: The definition of law; the first words of the sentence are left out.

full.html: A law, for Aquinas, has four marks: it is a rule of reason, not mere will; it aims at the common good, not one person's advantage; it is made by the one who has care of the community; and it is made public ("promulgated"), since a rule nobody knows cannot guide anyone.

full.name: gb-law-kinds
full.cap: Tap each kind of law. Eternal law contains the natural law, from which human laws are worked out; divine law, given in Scripture, stands alongside.

full.html: The natural law (Question 94) begins from a first rule that every practical mind knows: good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided. From our natural inclinations come further rules: to preserve our life, to raise and teach our children, to know the truth about God, and to live in society with others.

Human law (Questions 95 to 97) is worked out from the natural law in two ways. Some laws follow as conclusions ("do not murder" follows from "do no harm"). Others settle details that reason leaves open, such as a particular penalty, or which side of the road to drive on. Human law, he adds, should not try to forbid every vice, only the graver ones that harm others and that most people can avoid; and it may change as people and times change.

Thinking Aquinas held that any command from a ruler is a law. He argues that a human rule that goes against the natural law is not truly a law but a corruption of law, and that unjust laws do not bind in conscience, though one may still obey them to avoid scandal or disorder. This idea had a long history: Martin Luther King Jr. quoted Augustine and Aquinas on unjust laws in his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963). Legal philosophers who separate law from morality, such as John Austin and H. L. A. Hart, reject this view; the debate between the two schools goes on.
The Part ends with grace (Questions 109 to 114): the help Aquinas believes God gives so that people can reach an end beyond their natural powers.

deep.html: Much of this Part is a conversation with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, which Aquinas also wrote a commentary on. Both say happiness is the last end, that virtue is a habit and a mean, and that we become good by doing good acts. Aquinas adds what Aristotle did not have: a last end beyond this life, the theological virtues, and the eternal law. Readers still argue over whether he completes Aristotle or changes him.

Aquinas's questions on law became the classic statement of natural law theory. Later thinkers on this ladder, such as John Locke and the writers of the American founding, used natural law and natural rights in their own ways. Critics such as Jeremy Bentham called natural rights "nonsense upon stilts," and the legal positivists hold that what the law is and what it ought to be are separate questions.

items: Is there a last end that all people aim at, or does each person choose their own?
Can a law be unjust and still be a law? What would follow either way?
Should the law try to make people good, or only keep them from harming one another? Aquinas gives a middle answer. Do you agree?
Is a virtue really like a habit, or does goodness need to be chosen fresh each time?

deep.html: On this ladder, compare Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, then Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau on law and the common good.

questions: Make a list of things people think will make them happy. Which would Aquinas cross off, and why?
What is a habit you have worked to build? Did it get easier with practice?
Think of a rule at home or school. Does it pass Aquinas's four tests: reasonable, for everyone's good, made by the right person, and made known?
Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Can you name a time when someone was too cautious, or not cautious enough?
Why might a law not try to forbid every wrong thing?
care: This rung touches on questions of law and conscience. It presents Aquinas's views and those of his main critics, and takes no side.
